quote: Wie kann man eine gegebene Funktion am besten durch ein ganze Funktion [-von gegebenem der gege-] des gegebenen Körpers $(x, \sqrt{x^2+1})$ von gegebenem Grade darstellen?
english: How can one best represent a given function by an integral function of the given field (x, sqrt(x^2+1)) of given degree?
topic: Hilbert considers best approximation of a continuous function by integral functions of the field (x, sqrt(x^2+1)) of the form G(x)+H(x)sqrt(x^2+1), proposes an analogue of Gauss's orthogonality method with a candidate function built by repeated differentiation, and suggests generalizing to arbitrary algebraic function fields and continued fraction expansions.

triage.modern_statement: Fix a real interval (or a curve) and a weight. Let V_n be the finite-dimensional space of elements G(x) + H(x)·sqrt(x^2+1) of the integral closure of R[x] in the field R(x, sqrt(x^2+1)), with degree at most n (deg G ≤ n, deg H ≤ n−1, or a similar bound measured by pole order at infinity). Given a continuous f, find the element of V_n that best approximates f, in the least-squares (L^2) sense in Gauss's style. This means building an orthogonal basis of V_n, an analogue of the classical orthogonal polynomials, ideally given by a Rodrigues-type formula (repeated differentiation). Hilbert also suggested extending this to arbitrary algebraic function fields and linking it to continued-fraction expansions such as the expansion of sqrt(x^2+1). In modern terms this is the theory of orthogonal polynomials on algebraic curves, here the conic y^2 = x^2 + 1, a hyperbola.
triage.answered_by: I found no work that responds directly to Hilbert's note. In the least-squares form, the problem is projection onto a finite-dimensional space, so in principle it is routine. Explicit orthogonal bases have been worked out: for polynomials on quadratic curves, including the hyperbola, by Sheehan Olver and Yuan Xu ('Orthogonal structure on a quadratic curve', IMA J. Numer. Anal. 41 (2021) 206–246; arXiv 2018). The extension to higher-genus curves followed: Fasondini, Olver and Xu on planar cubic and elliptic curves (Found. Comput. Math., 2021), and later work on a class of planar algebraic curves. Bertola and others took up elliptic orthogonal polynomials with Riemann–Hilbert analysis. The continued-fraction side, the expansion of sqrt(D(x)) in hyperelliptic fields, goes back to Abel (1826) and Chebyshev, and is a well-studied classical topic. This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Olver and Xu studied orthogonal polynomials on quadratic curves in the plane, constructing an explicit orthogonal basis for any quadratic curve. Section 5 treats the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1, which matches Hilbert's field (x, sqrt(x^2+1)) after an affine change.

Published as Olver & Xu, Orthogonal structure on a quadratic curve, IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis 41(1), 2021, 206–246. The paper also covers convergence of the Fourier orthogonal series, i.e. best L^2 approximation.
Extension to higher-degree curves: Fasondini, Olver and Xu treat orthogonal polynomials in two variables on cubic curves, including elliptic curves.
Further extension: orthogonal polynomials on a class of planar algebraic curves.
Building on Bertola and on Fasondini–Olver–Xu, a class of orthogonal polynomials on elliptic curves is defined, with a Riemann–Hilbert framework (Constructive Approximation, 2024).
Active current work on elliptic orthogonal polynomials connects them with Padé approximation and Riemann–Hilbert asymptotics (2025 preprint).

The continued fraction of sqrt(D(t)) for a polynomial D was studied by Abel in 1826 and by Chebyshev in 1852. Its periodicity is linked to the polynomial Pell equation and to torsion points in (generalized) Jacobians.

triage.why: Hilbert's question, best approximation by integral functions G + H·sqrt(x^2+1) of bounded degree, with a Gauss-style orthogonality construction, is the least-squares problem for orthogonal polynomials on the conic y^2 = x^2 + 1. Recent work on orthogonal polynomials on quadratic curves (Olver–Xu 2021, hyperbola case included) solves this explicitly. Work on cubic, elliptic and more general algebraic curves (Fasondini–Olver–Xu; Bertola; 2024–2025 papers) carries out the generalization to arbitrary algebraic function fields that Hilbert proposed, and that area is active today. The continued-fraction side goes back to Abel and Chebyshev and is still studied. Caveats: I found no source citing Hilbert's note, so this is a match of the mathematics, not a documented line of influence. The note is also unclear on what 'best' means (least squares versus Chebyshev/uniform norm) and does not specify the interval or weight. I also could not check that his particular candidate built by repeated differentiation matches any published Rodrigues-type formula.
